newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives face by-election humiliation.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives face by-election humiliation.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives face assured humiliation when voters go to the polls on Thursday in a parliamentary by-election in one of the most run-down working-class constituencies in England.

But the Labour Party, while certain to make Prime Minister John Major's parliamentary position still less secure by winning the Barnsley East seat, will look nervously at the result when it is declared around 0030 gmt on Friday morning.

For if the newly-formed Socialist Labour Party, brainchild of pugnacious miners' union leader Arthur Scargill, polls well, the message will be that there is room in British politics for a party to the left of moderate opposition leader Tony Blair.

At the 1992 general election, Labour had a huge majority of 24,777 votes over the Conservatives in Barnsley East, a collection of former coal mining villages in Northern England whose pits have all closed causing high unemployment.
With Labour now some 20-30 points ahead of the Conservatives in national opinion polls, their candidate, local council leader Jeff Ennis, is virtually a certainty on Thursday.
"The nation owes a debt to places like Barnsley East, and the Tories now have to pay that debt," he told Reuters.

Conservative candidate Jane Ellison admits the electoral earthquake needed to make her an MP looks a remote possibility. But she said: "While there is a grudging acceptance that Labour had to change, there is no warmth here for Tony Blair."

It is the disappointment of old-style Labour supporters over Blair's rejection of traditional policies such as high taxes to fund generous welfare payments on which Socialist Labour candidate Ken Capstick's hopes are based.
"The Labour Party isn't on the side of working people any more," he told the Independent newspaper.
"Tony Blair believes he can move as far to the Right as he wants because those on the Left are his prisoners as they couldn't vote Tory. Now that's changed...they can vote for us."

Although election workers at Capstick's grimy headquarters in the village of Great Houghton speak of fighting to win, he would probably regard a 10 percent share of the vote as a triumph for a party only formally founded in March.

Some political analysts believe Capstick could make inroads into Labour's vote, although there are Barnsley voters who see Scargill as equally to blame for the rapid demise of Britain's mining industry as the Conservatives.
In 1984, Scargill led miners in a bruising year-long strike which aroused the ire of then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

Ennis's victory will put the Conservatives in a still more difficult position in parliament, where they lost their overall majority last Friday when a legislator angry about local hospital facilities withdrew his support from Major.
But although two other Conservatives have muttered threats to quit, Major is expected to soldier on until May before calling a general election he will be hard pressed to win.
